From Monday to 1935

Monday, Michener: where states got to choose, racial gaps followed

Today, Mettler: Congress faced that choice in 1935

What to run nationally? What to leave to the states?

Roosevelt signs the Social Security Act, Aug. 14, 1935 · FDR Library, CC BY 2.0

Michener 2020, pp. 550–51 · Mettler 1998, pp. 1–6

Mettler’s question

Before 1935: what citizenship meant was “defined primarily by the individual states”

New Deal: Washington steps in, but only for some

Structured governance (her method): look at how a program is designed and who runs it, then at what kind of citizens it makes

Think: a check from Washington, set by formula, vs. a county caseworker’s decision

Social citizenship: the right to basic economic security, as a member of the community

Mettler 1998, pp. 1–5, 9 · figure 1, p. 5

Divided citizenship

Redrawn from Mettler, table 1, p. 23 · labels from pp. 5, 23–25

Who counted as a worker?

1935: farm workers and domestic workers left out of Social Security and unemployment insurance

Domestic servants on relief, 1934: more than two-thirds Black

Mettler, pp. 20, 26 n. 78, 136 · Photos: Russell Lee, Oklahoma, 1939; Marion Post Wolcott, Atlanta, 1939 · FSA/OWI, Library of Congress

Building unemployment insurance

  • Perkins’s committee: unemployment insurance (UI) is “the cornerstone”
  • 3% federal payroll tax on employers; a state with its own UI law keeps 90%
  • So states set benefits and who qualifies
  • Built to replace “male breadwinners’” wages

Perkins, Jan. 22, 1935 · Harris & Ewing, LOC

Mettler, ch. 5, pp. 120–28, 136; ch. 6, p. 144

Building Aid to Dependent Children (ADC)

  • Designed by two Children’s Bureau women: Lenroot and Abbott
  • Run by the states; Washington pays ⅓
  • Congress cut the “decency and health” benefit standard
  • Benefit ceiling: $18 a month, first child; $12 each additional
  • For the mother herself: nothing (“no caretakers’ benefits”)

Federal Security Agency publicity print, 1940s · FSA/OWI, Library of Congress

Mettler, ch. 5, pp. 120, 129–40

1935: “fairly comparable ground”

UI ADC
Run by national and state together national and state together
Who qualifies: set by states states
Merit-based hiring required no no
Paid for by payroll tax on employers, held in Washington grants: $1 federal for every $2 state

Same start in 1935. What split them later: how each was paid for and run.

Mettler, table 4, p. 142; pp. 141–43

UI in practice: who qualifies?

To qualify: earn at least $100–300 a year (15 states, 1939)

More women than men earned too little

“Available for work” = full-time, daytime

Quit for family reasons (a “domestic quit”): no benefits

Mettler, ch. 6, pp. 150–53 · 1940 Census, cited

Pregnancy and marriage rules

Pregnant: disqualified, or ruled “unavailable” for work

Quit a job to marry: disqualified in 17 states by 1945

“UI acquired a janus-faced character”

Janus-faced = two-faced: a right for some, a barrier for others

Mettler, ch. 6, pp. 154–57, table 5

ADC in practice: it depended on where you lived

Dec. 1937: $10.40 a month in Arkansas, $61.16 in Massachusetts

“Suitable home” rules, caseworkers judging mothers: 31 of 45 states, 1941

Georgia: a racial quota on who got aid

Mettler, ch. 6, table 6, p. 160; pp. 164–72

1939: who moved up, who stayed

  • Widows of covered workers move up to Social Security
  • ADC gets a means test (“inscribed with means testing”)
  • Black share of ADC families: 14–17% in the late 1930s → 31% in 1948

Mettler: 1939 “rescued mostly white, middle-class women”

Social Security Board poster · FDR Library, National Archives

Mettler, ch. 6, pp. 167–69

Mettler’s conclusion

“it was their designs that propelled them toward their separate fates”

UI’s design → the same rules nationwide

ADC’s design → mothers as “vassals” of each state’s politics

Mettler, ch. 6, p. 175

Mettler and Michener, side by side

Mettler, 1935–1950 Michener, 2010–2020
Who gets sorted women from men, and by race by race, and by state
What does the sorting how programs were designed, then run a court ruling, state choices, waivers, appointees
How states got the power written into the 1935 law: who qualifies, benefits, morals rules opened by Sebelius in 2012; widened by waivers
Who is left to the states women, nonwhite men Black and Latino adults in the South
The author’s explanation “their designs” politics undoes policy

Paper 5: the same mechanism twice, or two that only look alike? Mechanism = the way a policy ends up sorting people

Paper 5: draft your position

With a partner, 6 minutes. Write down three things:

  1. Your position, in one sentence: are Mettler and Michener describing the same mechanism, or two different ones?
  2. Your evidence: one page number from Mettler and one from Michener.
  3. Your prediction: if you’re right, where should we see it next? Name a program.
